disease_info: Schizoaffective Disorder (Depressive Type) is characterized by an uninterrupted period of illness during which there is a major depressive episode concurrent with symptoms of schizophrenia, such as delusions, hallucinations, or disorganized behavior. To meet criteria, psychotic symptoms must also occur for at least two weeks in the absence of prominent mood symptoms, distinguishing it from mood disorders with psychotic features, while mood symptoms are present for a substantial portion of the total illness duration, distinguishing it from schizophrenia. The course is often chronic or recurrent, with functional impairment across work, social, and self-care domains, and it may follow major psychosocial stressors or progressive deterioration without an obvious trigger. Depressive-type presentations commonly involve pervasive low mood, loss of interest, and feelings of worthlessness alongside fixed, often distressing psychotic experiences.

narrative.personality: Gloria is a curious, socially engaged, art-driven developer who thrives on mentoring others and juggling multiple creative and technical projects, even if her planning is sometimes chaotic.
narrative.stressor: The onset of Gloria’s illness followed the sudden death of her husband, with whom she had shared decades of routines, financial decision-making, and emotional support, leaving her living alone for the first time in years. Initially she tried to cope by throwing herself into work, meetups, and mentoring, but her already flexible, somewhat disorganized habits slid into missed deadlines, forgotten bills, and increasing isolation when she found it harder to keep up with complex projects. Over the next two years, her sense of purpose eroded as she withdrew from hiking, concerts, and painting groups, spending long evenings alone ruminating on what his death meant and becoming increasingly preoccupied with rigid, unusual ideas about why it happened and what others thought about her. She ultimately sought psychiatric care after her mentees and a close friend from a senior-citizen circle noticed her growing preoccupation with these fixed beliefs, her marked decline in work reliability, and her inability to manage day-to-day tasks, urging her to see a doctor when she began insisting that something was profoundly wrong but could not explain it clearly.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I know people think I’m crazy, but these things I believe about what’s really going on around me are absolutely true, and no one will listen.”

narrative.personality: Irvin is a pragmatic, routine-driven man who prides himself on being reliable and carefully planning every aspect of his life, sometimes to an excessive and anxious degree.
narrative.stressor: Irvin’s difficulties began when a series of unexpected financial pressures hit in quick succession: his wife’s brief period of unemployment, a costly truck repair, and mounting anxiety about affording a mortgage they had just taken on. As someone who coped by over-planning and budgeting every detail, he responded by taking on extra shifts and obsessing over their finances, gradually sacrificing hobbies, sleep, and time with his wife to track bills and worst-case scenarios. Over the following two years, the constant stress eroded his confidence and sense of competence at work, and he became increasingly withdrawn and convinced that he was failing his family, interpreting minor mistakes or setbacks as proof that he was fundamentally defective. He finally agreed to psychiatric evaluation after his wife and supervisor both confronted him about his intense self-blame, his visible emotional decline, and his repeated insistence that his family would be better off without him despite their reassurances that he had not actually done anything wrong.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I feel like everything that’s gone wrong for my family is my fault, like I’ve ruined their lives and don’t deserve to be here.”

narrative.personality: Chenice is a quiet, meticulous, and creatively curious young woman who pours care into her work and love of natural materials, even if she can be a bit absentminded with her own routines.
narrative.stressor: Chenice’s problems began after she started taking on more demanding interior painting contracts, juggling tight deadlines, early start times, and expectations to manage jobs more independently than she had before. The pressure to prove herself, combined with irregular work hours and commuting between sites, gradually disrupted her usual rhythms of quiet mornings in the garden and evening art, leading her to stay up late planning designs and wake up early for jobs, with sleep becoming increasingly inconsistent. Over the next two years, the chronic sleep disruption and stress left her feeling worn down and detached from the things she used to enjoy, and she became more isolated, skipping book club and cultural events as it felt harder to keep up with conversations and responsibilities. She eventually sought psychiatric help, encouraged by a coworker and an aunt, when she reported that her sleep had become so disturbed that days blurred together, she could no longer reliably show up for jobs on time, and she felt something was deeply wrong with how her mind was functioning.
narrative.chief_complaint: “My sleep is completely messed up—I either can’t fall asleep at all or I’m sleeping at the wrong times, and it’s starting to ruin my life.”
